title: Two different questions about speed
objective: By the end of this lesson you can tell which of the two a given problem is about, explain why improving one often worsens the other, and recognise the same trade in systems far from the processor.

blocks.text: The pipeline lesson produced a result worth stating plainly: instructions did not get faster, yet the program did. That is only possible because 'faster' means two different things, and confusing them is behind a large share of bad performance decisions.

rows: How many finish per unit of time?
A queue is being worked through
Improved by roughly the stage count

blocks.title: They are not reciprocals
blocks.text: If one operation takes 5 units, it is tempting to conclude the system does 0.2 per unit. That is only true when operations run one at a time. In the pipeline, latency stayed at 5 cycles while throughput reached 1 per cycle — a factor of five apart. Whenever work overlaps, the two numbers separate, and knowing which one your problem cares about decides which you should improve.

rows: Throughput does not help one person waiting
A batch job over a million records
Nobody is watching an individual record
Total completion time is what counts
Late is as bad as not done

blocks.text: The last row introduces a third idea that neither number captures: a deadline. A frame delivered after its moment is worthless even though it was produced. That is the same reasoning the networking course gave for choosing UDP over TCP in a video call — late data has no value, so retransmitting it costs without benefiting.
Improving one at the other's expense

items: Batching improves throughput and worsens latency: each item waits for the batch to fill
Buffering does the same, deliberately, to keep a pipeline fed
A deeper pipeline raises throughput and leaves latency unchanged or slightly worse
Caching improves latency for repeated work and does little for a single first access
Adding parallel workers improves throughput; a single request is no faster

blocks.title: The classic mistake is optimising the one nobody asked about
blocks.text: A service whose users complain about slow responses is a latency problem, and adding more workers will not fix it — each request still takes as long. A build that takes too long overall is a throughput problem, and shortening one compilation step barely helps. Before optimising anything, say out loud which of the two numbers the complaint is about; the answer usually rules out most of the options.
The same trade elsewhere in these courses

rows: One byte at a time is responsive
Large blocks move far more data
A pool serves more requests overall
One round trip before any data

blocks.text: That table is a summary of five courses in one shape. The reason the same trade keeps appearing is that it is not about processors or networks — it is about what happens whenever work can overlap, and the choice of which number to optimise is always a statement about who is waiting.

blocks.title: Classify and measure
steps: For each row of the second table, state which number a user would notice
Write a program that processes items one at a time and time a single item
Add batching in groups of 100 and measure both single-item time and total time
Confirm that one got worse while the other got better, and by how much
Take a service or script you use and decide which number its complaints are about
For a pipeline of 5 stages, compute latency and throughput for 1 and for 1000 items
Explain why the ratio between them differs so much between the two cases
Find one place in your own code where a batch would help and one where it would hurt
blocks.expected: A measurement showing batching improving one number and worsening the other, and a decision about your own code that names which number matters. That naming step is the practical content of this lesson — most performance work goes wrong before any code is changed, by optimising the number nobody was complaining about.

cheatsheet: Latency: how long one operation takes. Throughput: how many finish per unit time
They are reciprocals only when operations do not overlap
In a 5-stage pipeline, latency stayed at 5 cycles while throughput reached 1 per cycle
Batching and buffering improve throughput and worsen latency
More parallel workers improve throughput; one request is no faster
A deadline is a third idea: late work can be worthless even though it completed
Name which number the complaint is about before optimising anything
The same trade appears in file I/O, thread pools, connection reuse and event loops

checkpoint.prompt: A pipeline gives 5-cycle latency and 1-per-cycle throughput. Why are those not contradictory?

choices.C: Five instructions are in progress at once
choices.D: One of them is measured wrongly, hence the mismatch

checkpoint.explanation: One completes each cycle while each still takes five. They are reciprocals only when work does not overlap. Overlapping is exactly what a pipeline does, which is why the two numbers separate by the stage count.

checkpoint.prompt: Users complain that a service feels slow to respond. What will adding more worker threads achieve?

choices.B: It depends on the number of cores and the queue depth
choices.C: Little — each request still takes as long

checkpoint.explanation: That is a latency complaint and workers improve throughput. More workers serve more requests at once. If the complaint is that one request feels slow, the number that must change is the time that request takes.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does batching improve throughput while worsening latency?

choices.A: Fixed per-operation costs are shared across many items, but each item waits for the batch to fill before anything happens
choices.B: It does not — it improves both

checkpoint.explanation: It is the same shape as reading a file in large blocks rather than byte by byte: fewer fixed costs paid, at the price of the first byte arriving later.

checkpoint.prompt: What does a deadline add that neither latency nor throughput captures?

choices.B: A limit on parallelism that caps the flow of work
choices.D: Work completed too late can be worthless

checkpoint.explanation: A late video frame is not a slow frame, it is a useless one. That is the same reasoning behind choosing UDP for a video call in the networking course.
